source.title: Bias of Stochastic Gradient Descent or the Architecture: Disentangling the Effects of Overparameterization of Neural Networks

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Conceptually tests how increasing width affects generalization by comparing SGD-trained networks with randomly sampled, perfectly fitting networks. Its width sweeps and architectures differ from V2's stated one-hidden-layer ReLU setup.
record.gate_note: The paper tests width and depth effects on natural-label binary classification, and compares SGD with random fitting networks. It does not test random-label memorization or the other mapped claim versions. Results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly tests V2's width–generalization relationship in a new setting: SGD-trained LeNet, five-layer MLP, and small ResNet models on low-sample binary image tasks. All retained models have zero training error, and even the narrowest LeNet can fit the training sets; widening improves held-out accuracy.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. In these low-sample binary tasks, widening improves SGD generalization while random fitting networks mostly do not improve, which the authors attribute to SGD's implicit bias. Increasing depth makes G&C worse and makes SGD stagnate or worsen, which they attribute primarily to architectural bias. They explicitly avoid claiming that depth is generally detrimental.
record.recipe_differences: Uses binary natural-label tasks and zero-training-error filtering to compare SGD with random fitting networks. Widths are varied in LeNet, MLP, and ResNet rather than the one-hidden-layer ReLU setting named in V2. Augmentation, weight decay, and sophisticated learning-rate schedules are avoided; SGD uses cross-entropy for 60 epochs, batch size 2, and a fixed learning rate.
record.method_sensitivity: SGD outcomes depend strongly on initialization: U[-1, 1] leads to suboptimal early stopping, while Kaiming initialization improves results. Width trends are compared across architecture and dataset; the G&C CIFAR10 LeNet result has a slight improvement up to width 2/6 in some settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Randomly sampled, perfectly fitting networks mostly retain similar test accuracy with increasing width; CIFAR10 LeNet improves up to width 2/6 and then largely stagnates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width benefits depend on how fitting networks are selected: SGD benefits more than random sampling in these tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing depth worsens G&C accuracy, while SGD accuracy stagnates or worsens depending on the task and architecture.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing depth can hurt generalization in low-sample binary classification even among perfectly fitting networks.

fits_no_version.finding: For LeNet on 16 MNIST 0-vs-7 examples, SGD accuracy improves from 83.6% with uniform [-1,1] initialization to 96.3% with proper initialization; G&C achieves 82.8% in the initial comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization can strongly affect SGD generalization after perfect training accuracy is reached.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 235, 2024
record.problems: The experiments are restricted to binary classification in a low-sample regime. Width results are primarily shown in figures, without extractable exact values in the supplied text. The paper notes that its G&C sampling cost limits the study.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted beyond the 8 listed. Other width figure panels repeat the reported trends for additional class pairs or sample counts; these are summarized in the existing rows rather than duplicating every plotted condition.

untested.parts: No own experiment fitting fixed random labels or comparing random-label and natural-label held-out accuracy.

The original one-hidden-layer setup, training to convergence, and behavior approaching or crossing the interpolation threshold are not tested. These experiments begin with networks already capable of fitting the data.
No controlled convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison or isolation of local connectivity, learned sparsity, or convolutional initialization.
No batch-size sweep or large-batch recipe comparison.
No magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness measurement or ranking of generalization gaps against competing measures.
No removal of memorized examples and retraining comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text states the width trends explicitly, so numerical plot values are unnecessary for the qualitative verdict. Random weights are not random labels, geometric margin is not magnitude-aware sharpness, and increasing depth does not challenge a claim specifically about increasing width.

versions.untested_parts: Does not train on random labels or compare held-out performance on random versus natural labels.
Uses LeNet, MLP, and ResNet width sweeps rather than one-hidden-layer ReLU networks; does not locate the interpolation threshold or report results specifically as width passes that threshold.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected architectures as a test of their relative image generalization.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD.
Does not vary batch size or compare large- and small-batch training.
Measures geometric margin and test accuracy, but does not test whether magnitude-aware sharpness ranks train-test gaps against other generalization measures.
